summary: Specifies the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol for sending traffic flow information from an exporting process to a collecting process. It defines how data and template records are carried, so the data format is described with it. It was replaced by RFC 7011.

plainLanguage.summary: IPFIX is how a router sends reports about the traffic that passed through it to a central collector. Each report describes a flow, a set of packets sharing the same properties. The exporter first sends a template that names the fields in its records, and then sends the records themselves.

questions: how are ip flow records exported
subtitle: The protocol that carries traffic flow records from the routers that measured them to the collector that stores them.

tldr.problem: Networks are made of flows, and an operator often needs to know what those flows were: how many bytes, between which addresses, over what period. Getting that information out of the network needs a common way to describe a flow and to carry it.
tldr.mechanism: IPFIX messages carry sets of records. A template set says which information elements a set of records holds and in what order, and a data set then carries the values. The exporter sends the template first, then the data, over SCTP, UDP or TCP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5101 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7011.

today: RFC 5101 was a Proposed Standard published in January 2008. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 7011.

sections.title: What IPFIX Exports
sections.content:
A data network with IP traffic primarily consists of IP flows passing through the network elements. It is often interesting, useful, or even required to have access to information about these flows for administrative or other purposes. The IPFIX Collecting Process should be able to receive the flow information passing through multiple network elements within the data network, which requires uniformity in the method of representing the flow information and the means of communicating the flows from the network elements to the collection point. This document specifies the protocol to achieve that, and describes in detail the representation of different flows, the additional data required for flow interpretation, the packet format, the transport mechanisms used and the security concerns.

Within IPFIX, a flow is a set of IP packets passing an observation point in the network during a certain time interval. All packets belonging to a particular flow have a set of common properties, and each property is defined as the result of applying a function to the values of one or more packet header fields, transport header fields or application header fields; one or more characteristics of the packet itself, such as the number of MPLS labels; and one or more fields derived from packet treatment, such as the next hop IP address or the output interface. A packet belongs to a flow if it completely satisfies all the defined properties of the flow.

An observation point is a location in the network where IP packets can be observed, for example a line to which a probe is attached, a shared medium such as an Ethernet-based LAN, a single port of a router, or a set of interfaces of a router. An observation domain is the largest set of observation points for which flow information can be aggregated by a metering process, and every observation point is associated with an observation domain. In the IPFIX message it generates, the observation domain includes its Observation Domain ID, which is unique per exporting process, so that the collecting process can identify the specific observation domain that metered the flows.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is a group of packets that look alike: same addresses, same ports, same treatment. IPFIX reports those groups, with the number of packets and bytes in each. The place the packets were seen is the observation point, and the group of such places a router meters together is the observation domain.

sections.title: The IPFIX Message and Its Header
sections.content:
An IPFIX Message consists of a Message Header followed by one or more Sets, and the Sets can be any of three types: Data Set, Template Set or Options Template Set. The Exporter MUST code all binary integers of the message header and the sets in network-byte order, which is big-endian byte ordering.

The message header has five fields. Version is the version of the flow record format exported in the message, and the value of this field is 0x000a for the current version, incrementing by one the version used in the NetFlow services export version 9. Length is the total length of the IPFIX message in octets, including the header and the sets. Export Time is the time in seconds since 0000 UTC Jan 1 1970 at which the message header leaves the exporter. Sequence Number is an incremental sequence counter modulo 2^32 of all IPFIX Data Records sent on this stream from the current observation domain, and the collecting process SHOULD use it to identify whether any data records have been missed; template and options template records do not increase the sequence number. Observation Domain ID is a 32-bit identifier of the observation domain that is locally unique to the exporting process, and it SHOULD be 0 when no specific observation domain is relevant for the whole message.

A Set is a generic term for a collection of records that have a similar structure. Each set consists of a Set Header and one or more records, and the record types must not be mixed within a set. The exporting process MAY insert padding octets so that the subsequent set starts at an aligned boundary; for security reasons the padding octets must be zero valued, and the padding length must be shorter than any allowable record in the set.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPFIX message opens with a fixed 16-byte header: the format version, the total length, the time it was sent, a counter of how many records have been sent, and which observation domain they came from. After that come the sets of records.

sections.title: Templates, Options and Data Records
sections.content:
One of the essential elements in the IPFIX record format is the Template Record, because templates allow the collecting process to process IPFIX messages without necessarily knowing the interpretation of all data records. A Template Record contains any combination of IANA-assigned and enterprise-specific information element identifiers, and consists of a Template Record Header and one or more Field Specifiers. The header holds the Template ID, which is unique within the transport session and observation domain that generated it, and the Field Count, the number of fields in the record. Template IDs 0 to 255 are reserved for template sets, options template sets and other reserved sets, and template IDs of data sets are numbered from 256 to 65535.

Each Field Specifier names one field of a record. It holds an enterprise bit, the information element identifier, the field length in octets, and, when the enterprise bit is set, the enterprise number of the authority that defined the identifier. When the enterprise bit is zero the identifier is an IETF-specified information element and the enterprise number must not be present; when it is one, the identifier is enterprise-specific and the enterprise number must be present. The value 65535 in the field length is reserved for variable-length information elements.

Thanks to the notion of scope, the Options Template Record gives the exporter the ability to provide additional information to the collector that would not be possible with flow records alone. An example is the Flow Keys option template, which reports the flow keys for a template, with the template itself defined as the scope; another is the template configuration, which reports the configuration sampling parameters for the template. The scope gives the context of the reported information elements in the data records, and multiple scope fields may be present, in which case the composite scope is the combination of the scopes.

Data Records are sent in Data Sets, and a data record consists only of one or more Field Values. The template the values belong to is identified by the Set ID field of the Set Header, which equals the Template ID. Field values are encoded according to their data type, and their length is not necessarily 16 bits. The interpretation of a data record can be done only if the template record corresponding to the template ID is available at the collecting process.
sections.plainLanguage: A template names the fields in a record and says how long each one is. The data set that follows holds the values, in that order, with no names of their own. A receiver that has the template can read the values; one that does not cannot.

sections.title: Template Management
sections.content:
The exporting process assigns and maintains the template IDs per SCTP association for the exporter's observation domains, and a newly created template record is assigned an unused template ID. If a specific information element is required by a template but is not available in observed packets, the exporting process may choose to export flow records without that information element in a data record defined by a new template. If an information element is required more than once in a template, the different occurrences should follow the logical order of their treatments by the metering process.

Template sets and options template sets may be sent on any SCTP stream, but they must be sent reliably using SCTP-ordered delivery, and the collecting process must store the template record information for the duration of the association so that it can interpret the corresponding data records. The exporting process SHOULD transmit the template set and options template set in advance of any data sets that use that template ID, to help ensure that the collector has the template record before receiving the first data record. Data records that correspond to a template record may appear in the same and subsequent IPFIX messages.

Templates that are no longer used should be deleted, and before reusing a template ID the template must be deleted. A template is withdrawn with a Template Withdrawal Message, which is a template record for that template ID with a field count of 0. The withdrawal message must not be sent until sufficient time has elapsed for the collecting process to receive and process the last data record using that template, a suitable default being 5 seconds after the last data record has been sent, and the template ID from a withdrawn template must not be reused until enough time has elapsed for the withdrawal message to arrive. If the measurement parameters change so that a new template is required, the template must be withdrawn and redefined, or an unused template ID must be used.

When the SCTP association shuts down or the exporting process restarts, all template assignments are lost and template IDs must be reassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The exporter keeps a list of the templates it has sent, and it tells the collector when a template is no longer used. The collector holds the template for as long as the session lasts, because it needs it to read the data records that arrive afterwards.

sections.title: Transport Protocols
sections.content:
The IPFIX protocol specification has been designed to be transport protocol independent, and an exporter can export to multiple collecting processes using independent transport protocols. The 16-bit Length field of the message header limits the length of an IPFIX message to 65535 octets including the header, and a collecting process must be able to handle message lengths of up to 65535 octets.

SCTP using the PR-SCTP extension must be implemented by all compliant implementations, while UDP and TCP may also be implemented. PR-SCTP SHOULD be used where exporters and collectors communicate over links that are susceptible to congestion, because it can provide any required degree of reliability. TCP MAY be used on such links, but PR-SCTP is preferred because of its ability to limit back pressure on exporters and its message rather than stream orientation. UDP MAY be used, although it is not congestion-aware, and in that case the IPFIX traffic between exporter and collector must run in an environment where it has been provisioned for or is contained by some other means.

Over UDP, messages may be lost, so UDP must not be used unless the application can tolerate some loss of IPFIX messages, and the collecting process should deduce the loss and reordering of data records from discontinuities in the sequence number. The maximum size of exported messages must be configured so that the total packet size does not exceed the path MTU, and if the path MTU is unknown a maximum packet size of 512 octets should be used. By default the collecting process listens on the UDP port 4739, and on UDP port 4740 for secure connections.

Over UDP, template sets and options template sets must be re-sent at regular intervals, since earlier copies may have been lost; the default for the frequency of that transmission is 10 minutes. Template withdrawal messages must not be used over UDP, as the method is inefficient given the unreliable nature of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX can run over three transports. SCTP is the one every implementation must have; UDP and TCP are optional. Over UDP, templates are sent again every ten minutes, because a datagram may simply have been lost.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The security requirements for IPFIX are three. IPFIX must provide a mechanism to ensure the confidentiality of IPFIX data transferred from an exporting process to a collecting process, to prevent disclosure of flow records. It must provide a mechanism to ensure the integrity of that data, to prevent the injection of incorrect data or control information such as templates into an IPFIX message stream. And it must provide a mechanism to authenticate IPFIX collecting and exporting processes, to prevent the collection of data from an unauthorized exporter or the export of data to an unauthorized collector.

The reason is that IPFIX can be used to collect information for network forensics and billing purposes, so attacks designed to confuse, disable or take information from an IPFIX collection system may be a prime objective during a sophisticated network attack. An attacker able to inject false messages can affect the application using IPFIX by falsifying data, or the collecting process itself by modifying or revoking templates or changing options. The messages may also contain information of value to an attacker, including the configuration of the network as well as end-user traffic and payload data, so their visibility must be confined to authorized users. When an information element containing end-user payload information is exported, it should be transmitted so that its contents are secure against eavesdropping, and it is the responsibility of the collecting process to provide a satisfactory degree of security for the data it collects, including anonymization where necessary.

Transport Layer Security and Datagram Transport Layer Security were designed to provide the confidentiality, integrity and authentication assurances IPFIX requires. With the mandatory SCTP and PR-SCTP transports, DTLS must be implemented; if UDP is selected, DTLS must be implemented; and if TCP is selected, TLS must be implemented. The RFC notes a weakness in DTLS over SCTP: a true man in the middle may take data out of an association and fool the sender into thinking the peer received it, and someone could inject SCTP control information to shut down the association.
sections.plainLanguage: Flow records say who talked to whom and how much, so they need protecting. The exporter and collector must be able to keep the records private, detect tampering and check each other's identity, which the RFC does with DTLS or TLS depending on the transport.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version of the flow record format exported in this message.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message in octets, including the header and the sets.

fields.name: Export Time
fields.desc: Seconds since 0000 UTC Jan 1 1970, when the header leaves the exporter.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Incremental counter modulo 2^32 of the data records sent from this observation domain.

fields.name: Observation Domain ID
fields.desc: 32-bit identifier of the observation domain, locally unique to the exporting process.
